timeline.title: Born near the volcanoes
timeline.text: Juana Inés de Asbaje y Ramírez was born in San Miguel Nepantla, near Mexico City, probably on 12 November 1648, to parents who were not married. A second baptism record points to 1651, and scholars still debate which is hers.

timeline.title: Reading before three
timeline.text: Before she was three, she followed her older sister to a small school and told the teacher, untruthfully, that her mother wanted her taught too. She learned to read so fast that she could read before her mother found out.

timeline.title: Her grandfather's books
timeline.text: At six or seven she heard that Mexico City had a university and begged her mother to let her go there dressed as a boy. Her mother said no, so she read the many books in her grandfather's library instead, though she was scolded for it.

timeline.title: A first poem
timeline.text: At about eight she wrote a poem for the feast of the Eucharist, according to her early biographers. She also learned Nahuatl from the people around her.

timeline.title: Teaching Latin
timeline.text: By thirteen she was teaching Latin to young children.

timeline.title: To the capital
timeline.text: At sixteen she went to live in Mexico City. She studied Latin grammar in fewer than twenty lessons, cutting her hair as a self-set deadline: if she had not learned a lesson before it grew back, she cut it again.

timeline.title: At the viceroy's court
timeline.text: She became a lady-in-waiting to the vicereine Leonor Carreto, wife of the Marquis of Mancera, and was admired at court for her poems and learning. She turned down offers of marriage.

timeline.title: Tested by the scholars
timeline.text: The viceroy gathered theologians, lawyers, philosophers and poets to question her. She answered them without preparation, and her fame grew.

timeline.title: A false start
timeline.text: She entered the strict convent of the Discalced Carmelites but left after only a few months.

timeline.place: Convent of San Jerónimo, Mexico City, New Spain, (Mexico)
timeline.title: A room of her own
timeline.text: She entered the Hieronymite convent of San Jerónimo and took the name Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz. She chose convent life because it let her study. She stayed for the rest of her life, building a large library and receiving scholars and poets.

timeline.title: The Allegorical Neptune
timeline.text: For the arrival of the new viceroy, the Marquis of la Laguna, and his wife María Luisa Manrique de Lara, she designed the meaning of a triumphal arch and explained it in a learned book, the Neptuno alegórico. The new rulers became her patrons.

timeline.title: A comedy for the court
timeline.text: Her comedy Los empeños de una casa (The Trials of a Household) was first performed on 4 October 1683, during celebrations for the birth of the viceroy's first child.

timeline.title: Her poems in print
timeline.text: Her friend María Luisa, Countess of Paredes, back in Spain, had her poems printed in Madrid as Inundación castálida. The book made her famous across the Spanish-speaking world.

timeline.title: A letter to her confessor
timeline.text: In a private letter now called the Autodefensa espiritual, she defended her studies to her confessor, Antonio Núñez de Miranda.

timeline.title: The bishop's letter
timeline.text: Bishop Manuel Fernández de Santa Cruz of Puebla published her private critique of a famous sermon by the Jesuit António Vieira, without her consent, as the Carta atenagórica. He added a letter, signed with the pen name Sor Filotea, urging her to turn away from worldly learning.

timeline.place: Convent of San Jerónimo, Mexico City, New Spain, (Mexico)
timeline.title: The Answer
timeline.text: She replied with the Respuesta a Sor Filotea. She told the story of her own self-education and argued, using the Bible and history, that women have the right to study. It is now one of her most famous works.

timeline.title: The Second Volume and First Dream
timeline.text: The second volume of her works was printed in Seville in 1692 and again in Barcelona in 1693. It included Primero sueño, her longest poem, about the soul trying to understand the whole universe during one night's sleep.

timeline.place: Convent of San Jerónimo, Mexico City, New Spain, (Mexico)
timeline.title: Silence
timeline.text: Under pressure from Church authorities she apparently stopped writing. Historians disagree about why: some see a sincere turn to religious life, others a campaign to silence a woman scholar.

timeline.place: Convent of San Jerónimo, Mexico City, New Spain, (Mexico)
timeline.title: The library is given up
timeline.text: Her name appears on a 1694 penance document signed "I, the worst of all", though its authenticity has been questioned. Her library of perhaps more than 4,000 books and her musical and scientific instruments were sold for charity, or by some accounts taken from her.

timeline.place: Convent of San Jerónimo, Mexico City, New Spain, (Mexico)
timeline.title: Death
timeline.text: An epidemic struck the convent. She caught the disease while caring for sick sisters and died on 17 April 1695. Her friend, the scholar Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora, gave the eulogy.

timeline.title: Fame and posthumous works
timeline.text: A third volume, Fama y obras póstumas, collected her last writings with tributes from admirers who called her the Phoenix of Mexico and the Tenth Muse.

timeline.title: Read again
timeline.text: The poet Octavio Paz published a major study of her life, translated into English in 1988 as Sor Juana, or, The Traps of Faith. She is now on Mexican banknotes, and her old convent houses the University of the Cloister of Sor Juana.

feature.title: Her works
feature.lead: Poems, plays, songs and letters, written in a convent cell between prayers and duties. Many first editions are free to read online.

items.label: Villancicos (carols)
items.text: Sets of songs written for church feasts and sung in Mexico City's cathedral. This printed set of 1676 was for the feast of the Immaculate Conception.

items.label: Neptuno alegórico
items.text: A learned prose book explaining the triumphal arch she designed for the new viceroy, picturing him as Neptune.

items.label: Los empeños de una casa
items.text: A lively comedy of mix-ups between two pairs of lovers, first staged for the viceroy's family.

items.label: Hombres necios (Foolish Men)
items.text: Witty verses accusing men of blaming women for faults that men themselves cause. Printed in Inundación castálida.

items.label: Inundación castálida
items.text: The first collection of her poems, printed in Spain through her friend the Countess of Paredes.

items.label: El divino Narciso
items.text: A religious allegorical play (auto sacramental), one of three she wrote, with a prologue (loa) that was also printed on its own.

items.label: Amor es más laberinto
items.text: One of her plays for the court, a comedy whose title means Love Is a Greater Labyrinth.

items.label: Carta atenagórica
items.text: Her sharp critique of a sermon by the Jesuit António Vieira, published by the bishop of Puebla without her consent.

items.label: Respuesta a Sor Filotea
items.text: Her answer to the bishop: the story of her self-education and a defence of women's right to learn.

items.label: Primero sueño (First Dream)
items.text: Her longest poem, following the soul on a night journey to understand everything. Often called the only work she wrote purely for herself.

items.label: Segundo tomo (Second Volume)
items.text: The second volume of her works, with First Dream, plays and the Carta atenagórica.

items.label: Fama y obras póstumas
items.text: The posthumous third volume, including the Respuesta and tributes to the Tenth Muse.
